mcqs.question: Why do webhook providers typically implement at-least-once delivery (retry with backoff) rather than at-most-once (try once, give up on failure)?
options: At-most-once is technically impossible to implement over HTTP
Retrying is required by HTTP itself for any POST request
Losing an event silently (e.g. a missed payment.succeeded) is usually far worse for the consumer than occasionally receiving a duplicate they can detect and ignore
At-least-once delivery guarantees events always arrive in the correct order
mcqs.explanation: The deliberate tradeoff is favoring 'might duplicate' over 'might silently lose' an event, since a missed critical event is usually the costlier failure mode for the consumer. At-most-once is entirely possible to implement (just don't retry); HTTP doesn't mandate retries on POST; and at-least-once delivery explicitly does NOT guarantee ordering, which is exactly why the following slide covers idempotent, order-tolerant consumers.

mcqs.question: A consumer verifies an incoming webhook's HMAC signature by first parsing the JSON body into an object, re-serializing it, and computing the HMAC over that re-serialized string. What's the likely problem?
options: There's no problem — HMAC verification works the same regardless of how the body is represented
HMAC signatures don't work with JSON payloads at all
The problem is only that parsing adds latency, not that verification could fail
Re-serialization can change formatting details (key order, whitespace), causing a genuinely valid signature to appear to fail because the bytes no longer match what the provider signed
mcqs.explanation: HMAC signs the exact raw bytes the provider sent; if the consumer re-serializes before verifying, even a semantically identical payload can produce different bytes and thus a different computed signature, causing a false verification failure. HMAC works fine with JSON payloads; the issue is specifically about byte-for-byte fidelity, not just performance overhead.

mcqs.question: A provider needs to notify an open browser tab of live updates. The browser cannot accept inbound HTTP connections. Which delivery mechanism fits, based on the compare slide?
options: SSE or WebSocket — a live, connected client can receive pushed updates over a connection it initiated outbound
A traditional webhook, since it's the fastest option regardless of client type
Polling only, since browsers can never receive push notifications of any kind
None of these work for browser clients under any circumstance
mcqs.explanation: The compare slide specifically notes SSE/WebSocket fit a live, already-connected client like a browser tab better than webhooks, since the browser initiates the connection outbound and the server pushes over it — no inbound reachability needed. A traditional webhook requires the consumer to expose a reachable public endpoint, which a browser can't do; polling is a fallback, not the best fit when a persistent connection is available.

mcqs.question: A webhook delivery system uses one shared worker pool across all merchants. One merchant's endpoint starts hanging on every request. What happens to delivery for other, healthy merchants?
options: Nothing — other merchants' deliveries are handled by entirely separate infrastructure automatically
The hanging endpoint can occupy every available shared worker, starving delivery to every other merchant even though their endpoints are healthy
Only that one merchant is affected; shared worker pools inherently isolate failures per consumer
The system automatically detects the slow endpoint and permanently blocks that merchant with no further impact
mcqs.explanation: A shared worker pool has no built-in isolation: a hanging endpoint holds a worker open until it times out, and if enough workers are tied up waiting on the same slow merchant, healthy merchants' deliveries queue up behind them with no capacity left to serve. There's no automatic separate infrastructure or automatic blocking unless it's explicitly built — the whole point of the pitfall is that this doesn't happen by default.
